note: Paraphrased fact cards for grounded answers. 'official' = U.S. government source. Cite by id. Facts were checked against each source on 2026-10-24; re-check before relying on them after the hackathon.

sources.title: Building credit from scratch (checklist)
facts: A secured credit card is applied for like a regular card, but you put down a deposit and the credit line generally matches that deposit.
You can generally build credit with a secured card, but you should ask the issuer whether it reports to the credit reporting companies.
Some secured cards let you move to a traditional (unsecured) card later.
Credit builder loans, usually offered by credit unions, are another way to start a credit history.
Paying credit card bills and loan payments on time is one of the most important steps in building good credit.
Using too much of your available credit can hurt scores, so stay well below your credit limit.
Opening too many credit accounts in a short time may lower credit scores.
You are entitled to request your credit report from each of the three nationwide credit reporting companies.

sources.title: Who are the credit invisible?
facts: A secured card deposit can range from about $50 to $300 depending on the card company.
Banks typically report secured card activity to the credit reporting companies, but you should confirm with the issuer.
Many secured cards include a 'graduation' feature that moves you to a traditional card after a pattern of on-time payments.
sources.caveat: Archived CFPB page; deposit ranges may have changed.

sources.title: I was an authorized user on my deceased relative's credit card account. Am I liable to repay the debt?
facts: Being an authorized user generally does not make you legally responsible for paying the account's debt.
Credit card issuers usually report an authorized user's status to the credit bureaus.
You can get a free copy of your credit report from each of the three nationwide bureaus at annualcreditreport.com.

sources.title: Credit Where None Is Due? Authorized User Account Status and 'Piggybacking Credit'
facts: Because of how authorized user accounts are reported, the account's full history can show up on the authorized user's credit record, no matter when they were added.
Adding someone as an authorized user has been used to help young people build a credit history and learn to manage credit.
Paying a stranger to be added to their account ('piggybacking') is a separate practice that has raised concerns.
sources.caveat: Research paper from 2010; scoring models may treat authorized users differently today.

sources.topic: Authorized users: minors and issuer rules
sources.title: Which Credit Cards Help Authorized Users Build Credit?
facts: Issuers commonly report authorized user accounts, but they are not required to.
Depending on their policies, credit bureaus may leave an authorized user account off the report if it has negative information or if the user is under a certain age.
At least one major issuer (Chase) says it does not report authorized user history for minors.
If the account isn't showing up on the authorized user's report, call the issuer and ask.
sources.caveat: Not a government source. Issuer policies change; always tell users to confirm with their card issuer.

sources.title: Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
facts: An ITIN is a 9-digit number the IRS issues for federal tax purposes to people who need a taxpayer ID but aren't eligible for a Social Security number.
An ITIN does not authorize work in the U.S., does not provide or change immigration status, and does not qualify someone for Social Security benefits or the Earned Income Tax Credit.
An ITIN is not meant to serve as identification outside the federal tax system.
You may need an ITIN if you must file a federal tax return, or if you can be claimed as a spouse or dependent for a tax benefit.
If you earned income but don't owe tax or aren't required to file, you may want to file a tax return anyway to get money back, such as a refund or refundable tax credit.

sources.title: If I am not a U.S. citizen, can I get a Social Security number? / Social Security Numbers for Noncitizens
facts: In general, only noncitizens with permission to work from the Department of Homeland Security can get a Social Security number.
Noncitizens who are not authorized to work can get an SSN only in limited cases; details are in SSA's 'Social Security Numbers for Noncitizens' publication (ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10096.pdf).

sources.title: H-4 Dependents
sources.publisher: Temple University International Student & Scholar Services; Utah State University HR
facts: H-4 status is available to the spouse and unmarried children under 21 of an H-1B worker, and it depends on the H-1B worker keeping valid status.
When an H-4 child turns 21, they are no longer considered a 'child' for this purpose and are no longer eligible for H-4 status.
H-4 children are not eligible to apply for work authorization (an EAD); only certain H-4 spouses can.
H-4 dependents may study in the U.S.
Dependents approaching 21 should talk to an immigration professional about other status options.
sources.caveat: University international offices, not USCIS. The app must FLAG this milestone and refer to an immigration attorney or school international office. Never give immigration advice.

sources.title: Growing Concern Over H-4 Dependent Children
facts: Long employment-based green card backlogs put many H-4 children at risk of aging out at 21.
In some cases the Child Status Protection Act (CSPA) may let a dependent keep 'child' classification for a time after turning 21.
Changing to F-1 student status while attending college is another path some H-4 children use.
sources.caveat: Law firm blog. Use only to say 'options exist and depend on your case, so talk to an immigration attorney early.' Do not explain eligibility.

sources.title: Reminder: Proof of Financial Support Needed to Issue Form I-20
sources.publisher: Study in the States (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)
facts: Prospective F-1 students must show they have the financial resources to live and study in the U.S.
A school official cannot issue the Form I-20 without proper proof of financial support, and students need the I-20 for the steps to study in F-1 status.
The funds shown should cover up to one year or the length of the program, whichever is shorter.
The cost information on the I-20 covers tuition, school fees, and living expenses.
sources.caveat: DHS marks these blog posts as possibly outdated. Schools set their own cost estimates and document rules.

sources.title: Non-U.S. Citizens (Financial Aid Toolkit) / Eligible noncitizen definition
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid; Eastern Kentucky University
facts: Students who are neither U.S. citizens nor 'eligible noncitizens' are not eligible for federal student aid.
Eligible noncitizens generally include green card holders and people with certain statuses such as refugee or asylee.
Students in the U.S. on F-1/F-2 or J-1/J-2 visas are not eligible noncitizens for federal student aid.
A parent's immigration status is not considered when deciding whether the student is eligible.
StudentAid.gov/noncitizen lists the categories that qualify.
sources.caveat: Some states and colleges offer their own aid to students who don't qualify for federal aid; rules vary widely. Tell users to check with the school's financial aid office.

sources.title: Avoiding scams that target immigrants
facts: In the U.S., notarios (notaries) are not licensed attorneys and cannot give legal advice on immigration.
Official immigration forms from USCIS are free; anyone charging for blank forms is a scammer.
Never sign blank forms or forms with information that isn't true.
Nobody can guarantee a green card or citizenship.
Get immigration information from websites ending in .gov.
Report immigration scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (Spanish: ReporteFraude.ftc.gov).

sources.title: Making a difference in the lives of immigrants and others who send money abroad
facts: Money transfer providers must generally disclose the exchange rate, fees, the amount that will arrive, and the date it will be available, both before and after you pay.
You typically have at least 30 minutes after paying to cancel an international transfer and get your money back.
If you report a problem within 180 days, the provider must generally investigate and correct errors.

sources.topic: Finding trustworthy human help with money
sources.title: Choosing a Credit Counselor
facts: Most reputable credit counselors are nonprofit and offer help in person, online, or by phone.
Universities, credit unions, military bases, and Cooperative Extension offices often run nonprofit credit counseling programs.
Calling itself 'nonprofit' doesn't guarantee a counselor is free, affordable, or legitimate.
Check a counseling organization with your state Attorney General and local consumer protection agency.

sources.title: Immigrants facing unique financial challenges
facts: People with limited English can struggle to get understandable information about financial products, compare costs, and correct errors.
Many rely on friends and family, often their minor children, to interpret financial transactions, which raises the risk of poor decisions.
Language barriers can put people at higher risk of scams that target immigrants.
CFPB publishes free 'Newcomer's Guides to Managing Money' in several languages.

sources.title: Visa codes for New York State residency (tuition)
sources.publisher: University at Buffalo (SUNY) Student Accounts; Washington State University Residency Office
facts: At the University at Buffalo (SUNY), students on visas that permit them to establish a U.S. residence may be eligible for in-state tuition, and H-4 is on its eligible list.
At the University at Buffalo, F-1 student visas are on the list of visas that are not eligible for in-state tuition.
Washington State University also lists F visas among those that can't be used to establish residency for tuition.
Washington State University warns students to consult its international programs office before applying for residency, because applying can negatively affect future immigration benefits.
sources.caveat: Two universities' rules, not federal law. In-state tuition rules differ by state and school. Always tell users to ask the college's residency office and international office.

sources.title: Working in the United States
sources.publisher: Study in the States (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)
facts: F-1 students who work on campus may not work more than 20 hours per week while school is in session.
Off-campus work for F-1 students requires a completed academic year and an economic hardship, plus approval from the school official and a Form I-765 filed with USCIS.
F-1 students can't begin off-campus work while the Form I-765 is pending with USCIS.

sources.title: Options for Nonimmigrant Workers Following Termination of Employment
facts: After a job ends, workers in H-1B and some other work statuses, and their dependents, may get a grace period of up to 60 days, or until their authorized stay ends if that comes sooner.
The grace period is discretionary.
Options USCIS lists include a new employer filing a petition, changing to another status, applying for a green card if eligible, or leaving the U.S.
Not all of these options give permission to work.
After an involuntary job loss, the employer of an H-1B worker must generally pay for return transportation.

sources.title: Free tax return preparation for qualifying taxpayers (VITA)
facts: The IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) program offers free tax return preparation.
Many VITA sites help people who generally earn about $70,244 or less, people with disabilities, and limited-English-speaking taxpayers.
The IRS doesn't set a program-wide income limit, but individual sites may set their own.
Some VITA sites also offer ITIN application services.
Services vary by site. Find one with the IRS VITA Locator Tool or by calling 800-906-9887.

sources.topic: Free and low-cost immigration legal help
sources.title: Recognized Organizations and Accredited Representatives Roster; List of Pro Bono Legal Service Providers
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR)
facts: The Justice Department keeps a roster of recognized organizations and accredited representatives that you can search by state.
The Justice Department also publishes a list of free (pro bono) legal service providers for people in immigration court proceedings.
